text: Some questions have a yes or no answer. Will this email turn out to be spam, given how many suspicious words it contains? We could label spam as one and normal mail as zero and fit a straight line, as in the last lesson, but a line keeps climbing forever, so it soon predicts values above one and below zero, which make no sense as chances. What we want is a curve that rises like a line in the middle but never leaves the range from zero to one.

That curve is the sigmoid. It takes any number z and returns one over one plus e to the minus z. Think of it as a dimmer switch rather than an on-off switch: very negative inputs leave the light almost off, very positive inputs turn it almost fully on, and an input of zero sets it exactly halfway. Because the output always lies between zero and one, we can read it as a probability.

Logistic regression keeps the linear part we already know and feeds it through the sigmoid. First compute a score, z equals w times x plus b, then the probability of spam is the sigmoid of that score. The score itself has a name worth remembering, the logit, and it measures the log of the odds. With two features the score is zero along a straight line, so the model splits the plane with a straight boundary, and the sigmoid only decides how confident it is on either side.

The weights control the shape of that confidence. A larger weight makes the curve steeper, so the model switches from no to yes over a narrow band, while a small weight spreads the change over a wide, uncertain region. Flipping the sign of the weight flips which side counts as yes, and changing the intercept slides the halfway point left or right.

To learn those weights we need a loss that suits probabilities. Squared error is a poor fit here, so instead we use the log loss, also called cross-entropy: when the true answer is one, the loss is minus the log of the predicted probability, and when it is zero, minus the log of one minus that probability. Think of it as a bet. Predicting point nine for something that happens costs little, but predicting point zero one for something that happens costs a great deal, and the penalty grows without limit as a confident prediction turns out wrong.

The reward for choosing this loss is a remarkably tidy gradient. For each example, the gradient with respect to the weights is simply the prediction minus the label, times the input. So an example that is already predicted well barely moves the weights, while a badly misjudged example pulls hard, and gradient descent, step after step, rotates and slides the boundary until the two groups sit on opposite sides.

A language model faces the same kind of question, only with tens of thousands of possible answers instead of two. Its final layer produces one score for every token in the vocabulary, still called logits, and the softmax function, the many-class cousin of the sigmoid, turns them into probabilities, trained with the very same cross-entropy loss. Next, we ask what happens when a model fits its training data too well.
